blocks.title: The nervous system
blocks.md:
The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the **brain** and **spinal cord**. **Nerves** carry electrical impulses between the CNS and the rest of the body. **Receptors** detect stimuli; **effectors** (muscles and glands) carry out the response.

Three types of **neurone**: **sensory** (receptor to CNS), **relay** (inside the CNS) and **motor** (CNS to effector). The gap between two neurones is a **synapse**, crossed by chemical transmitter.

blocks.title: Reflex action
blocks.md: A **reflex action** is a fast, automatic response to a stimulus that does not need thought. It protects the body (pulling the hand from a hot pot, blinking, the pupil narrowing). The path it follows is the **reflex arc**.

blocks.caption: The reflex arc, step by step.
blocks.alt: A vertical flow of seven boxes: stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the spinal cord, motor neurone, effector muscle and response.

blocks.title: Reflex versus voluntary action
blocks.md:
- **Reflex**: automatic, very fast, involves the spinal cord (or brainstem), not learned.
- **Voluntary**: you decide; the brain is involved; slower; can be learned (writing, walking, kicking a ball).

The brain's **cerebrum** controls thought and voluntary action; the **cerebellum** controls balance and coordination; the **medulla** controls breathing and heart rate.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A reflex is quick because there are few neurones and no decision, *not* because impulses are faster.
- Sensory neurones carry impulses *to* the CNS; motor neurones carry them *away*.
- The effector is the muscle or gland, not the nerve.

blocks.title: Name the path
blocks.statement: Describe the reflex arc when a person in Buea touches a very hot cooking pot.
steps: Receptors in the skin detect the heat and send impulses along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord.
A relay neurone passes the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to the arm muscle (effector); the muscle contracts and the hand is pulled away.
blocks.answer: Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.

blocks.title: Reflex or voluntary?
blocks.statement: Classify: (a) blinking when dust enters the eye, (b) writing a letter, (c) saliva when smelling frying plantain.
steps: (b) a decision of the brain: voluntary.

blocks.title: The eye
blocks.md:
- **Cornea**: transparent front; refracts (bends) light.
- **Iris**: coloured muscle that controls the size of the **pupil**.
- **Lens**: changes shape to focus light on the retina.
- **Retina**: contains light receptors: **rods** (dim light) and **cones** (colour, bright light).
- **Optic nerve**: carries impulses to the brain.
- **Ciliary muscles** and **suspensory ligaments** hold and change the lens.

blocks.caption: Section through the eye (schematic).
blocks.alt: A round eyeball with a transparent cornea at the front, a lens behind the pupil, the iris above and below the pupil, a red retina on the back wall and an optic nerve leaving the back.

blocks.title: Pupil reflex and accommodation
blocks.md:
**Pupil reflex**: in bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and the pupil gets smaller (protects the retina); in dim light the radial muscles contract and the pupil widens.

**Accommodation** (focusing):
- **Near object**: ciliary muscles contract, ligaments slacken, lens becomes thicker and more curved.
- **Distant object**: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments are taut, lens is thin.

blocks.title: The ear
blocks.md: Sound waves are collected by the **pinna** and travel along the ear canal to the **eardrum**, which vibrates. Three small bones (**ossicles**) pass and increase the vibrations to the **cochlea**, where receptor cells send impulses along the **auditory nerve** to the brain. The **semicircular canals** detect head movement for **balance**. The **Eustachian tube** equalises air pressure.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The *retina*, not the lens, contains the light receptors.
- A *thick* lens focuses *near* objects.
- The cochlea is for hearing; the semicircular canals are for balance.
- Do not push objects into the ear; loud noise can damage hearing (health review).

blocks.title: Bright light
blocks.statement: You walk out of a dark room into the sun at noon in Douala. Describe what happens to your pupils and why.
steps: Bright light is the stimulus; receptors in the retina send impulses to the brain and then to the iris.
The circular muscles of the iris contract, making the pupil smaller, so less light reaches the retina.
blocks.answer: The pupils narrow to protect the retina.

blocks.title: Reading a book
blocks.statement: You look from the blackboard to your notebook. How does the lens change?
steps: The notebook is a near object.
The ciliary muscles contract and the suspensory ligaments slacken, so the lens becomes thicker and bends light more to focus it on the retina.

blocks.title: Hormones
blocks.md: A **hormone** is a chemical substance made in an **endocrine gland** and carried by the **blood** to **target organs**, where it changes their activity. Examples: **insulin** and glucagon (pancreas), **adrenaline** (adrenal glands), **ADH** (pituitary), **testosterone** (testes), **oestrogen** and progesterone (ovaries).

blocks.title: Nerves compared with hormones
blocks.md:
- **Nerves**: electrical impulses along neurones; very fast; short-lasting effect; to a precise place.
- **Hormones**: chemicals in the blood; slower; longer-lasting effect; may act on several organs.

**Adrenaline** prepares the body for 'fight or flight': the heart beats faster, breathing increases, pupils widen and the liver releases glucose.

blocks.caption: Nerves and hormones compared.
blocks.alt: Two boxes: nerves with fast electrical impulses and a short effect; hormones with chemicals in the blood, slower and longer lasting.

blocks.title: Plant responses (tropisms)
blocks.md:
A **tropism** is a growth response of a plant to a directional stimulus. Plant hormones called **auxins**, made at the shoot tip, control it.

- **Phototropism**: shoots grow towards light. Auxin moves to the shaded side, making cells there elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.
- **Gravitropism**: roots grow downwards (positive); shoots grow upwards (negative).

blocks.caption: A shoot grows towards the light.
blocks.alt: A straight shoot in no light and a second shoot that bends to the right towards arrows representing light coming from the right.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Hormones do *not* travel in nerves; they travel in the *blood*.
- Auxin makes cells on the *shaded* side grow *longer*; it does not make the lit side shrink.
- Plants have no nerves or glands; their hormones move from cell to cell.

blocks.title: Fight or flight
blocks.statement: A boy meets a barking dog and his heart pounds. Name the hormone and two effects.
steps: The adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood.
Heart rate and breathing rate increase; the liver releases glucose for energy.
blocks.answer: Adrenaline; faster heart rate and more glucose in the blood.

blocks.title: Seedling on a window
blocks.statement: A maize seedling on a window sill in Limbe leans towards the window. Explain.
steps: Light from one side is the stimulus (phototropism).
Auxin collects on the shaded side, cells there elongate faster, so the stem bends towards the light.
blocks.answer: Unequal auxin distribution causes bending towards the light.
